papers.title: Meituan-Robotics-0: A Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Desktop Manipulation
papers.abstract: We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. MR0 combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. A three-stage training recipe aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior through discrete action-token pre-training, transfers these priors to continuous cross-embodiment control through flow-matching mid-training, and adapts the policy through real-world post-training. We introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections to provide positive and negative supervision for CFG-DAgger without value learning or advantage labeling. A unified end-effector interface supports heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. An event-driven agent maintains persistent task events and reassesses plans when progress or feasibility changes, enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than $\pi_{0.5}$ across three real-robot tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90. Qualitative agent deployments demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions.

papers.title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
papers.abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through analyzing intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Building on these insights, we propose Q-OIL, a method that adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning and softly guides exploration toward human corrections. We find that decoupled critics are critical for stability because they prevent the bonuses from backing up to pre-intervention states. As a result, Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improving pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks. As we ground both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.

papers.title: Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists
papers.abstract: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI. papers.title: Augmentron: Scalable Multi-View Visual Augmentation for Robot Learning
papers.abstract: Robot policies trained on visually narrow demonstrations can become sensitive to environmental features that are unrelated to the task. Existing generative augmentation methods can introduce visual diversity, but processing every frame and camera view independently is computationally expensive and may produce inconsistent observations across cameras and timestamps. We introduce Augmentron, a geometry-aware pipeline that generates reusable scene representations and renders them through recorded camera poses. This produces temporally and multi-view consistent environ- ment and workspace variations while preserving the robot, task objects, actions, and annotations. Across three physical manipulation tasks, replacing half of the real world training dataset with Augmentron data improves model success across three tasks for both in out-of-distribution distractor objects, and out-of-distribution workspace variation evaluations. In a separate comparison against alternate augmentation techniques, Augmentron achieves the highest pooled success in all three conditions. The results show that introducing augmented data to a data training recipe can help policies generalize to dynamic real-world settings.

papers.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
papers.abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.

papers.title: Ordered Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.

papers.title: HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields
papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

papers.title: Open-HumanWAM: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanWAM, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanWAM-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

executive_summary: Several vision-language-action foundations and training recipes are introduced: Open-HumanWAM scales egocentric human video pretraining to a 50,000-hour Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus and reports log-linear scaling between pretraining hours and downstream robot success, with HumanWAM-Goal joint human–robot pretraining achieving state-of-the-art RoboTwin 2.0 post-trained success (92.70% Clean2Clean, 84.60% Clean2Random) and showing in-context adaptation to unseen visual goals on physical robots; MR0 presents a three-stage VLA foundation model trained on 147M vision-language samples and 15,060 hours of trajectories across 12 embodiments, reaching 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and strong Ethernet insertion performance (70% success, 0.90 progress) with Rollback-based CFG-DAgger; A2-MEAS introduces an embodied multi-agent framework where correction codes train and adapt A2-WLA, which attains a 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success on BEHAVIOR 2026, 93.98–95.05% RoboTwin 2.0 success, and 57.92% success on 12 real-robot household tasks versus 26.67% for π₀.₅; and VICTR proposes an in-context value function estimator for progress-aware demonstration retrieval, improving a post-trained π₀.₅ policy on out-of-domain real-world manipulation from 6.2% to 23.8% success and from 28.9% to 55.5% average task progress relative to a fine-tuned baseline.

New methods target safer or more efficient policy adaptation from structured signals: CS-Pi combines projection and rejection for constraint-satisfying sampling in flow-matching policies, increasing safe success on a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place from 55% (pure projection) to 81% and zero-shot Franka hardware safe success from 40% to 55% while maintaining policy plausibility; Q-OIL models empirically observed progress-based human interventions and adds optimistic bonuses on intervention transitions with decoupled critics, yielding 10–50% higher success than baselines in simulation and real-robot experiments and improving pretrained vision-language-action agents on two bimanual tasks; and a weight-space programming approach has GPT-6 Astra edit 65 token-embedding rows of a robot policy to repair lexical grounding without gradients or new demonstrations, raising π₀.₅ success on 765 paraphrased instructions from 86.3% to 92.0% in the best run (48 repairs, 4 regressions) and from 74.3% to 87.5% on instructions containing edited tokens, with controls suggesting targeted lexical repair rather than broad new capabilities.

Several works contribute data, benchmarks, and augmentation pipelines for embodied intelligence: Open-HumanWAM releases an open, densely annotated 50,000-hour egocentric human video corpus with hand motion and language labels plus curation and pretraining pipelines; Augmentron provides a geometry-aware visual augmentation system that re-renders 3D scene representations along original camera trajectories, and on three physical manipulation tasks shows that replacing half the real data with Augmentron data improves success under in-distribution and out-of-distribution distractors and workspace changes, outperforming alternative augmentations in pooled success; ToolDex offers a large-scale egocentric–exocentric human tool-use dataset with multi-view sensing and detailed hand/tool/object/deformation annotations, defining benchmarks for tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D/4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning; Flex-RSI defines a recursive self-improvement benchmark where an improver edits the agent harness under a fixed budget, and analyses indicate that self-editing prompts/tools/memory/control loops substantially contribute to performance gains and that open-weight models struggle when only success/failure feedback or strict physical/exactness checks are present; and Seeing What Matters introduces a task-conditioned actionable spatial-belief benchmark where a diagnostic pipeline reaches ~99% success while seven vision-language models achieve only 26–43%, highlighting the importance of functional information and command binding and that view selection should be judged by task-relevant evidence coverage rather than scene completeness.

Planning, navigation, and perception for challenging environments are advanced by several methods: TPS-A* plans with certified collision checking using a trajectory-parameter lattice for exact, possibly non-convex footprints, solving all 300 cluttered-world queries in a median 3 ms while an exact checker finds no collisions and hybrid A* incurs 45% obstacle overlap, and achieving up to 89× speedups on position-only goals over hybrid A*; Execution-Grounded Traversability learns a flow-matching model over terrain and vehicle-contact features to estimate the probability of successful path execution, reducing safe-path rejection to 2.2% and unsafe-path acceptance to 7.7% in 650 simulated trials and lowering navigation failure rates by 24–44 percentage points and goal time by up to 45% when embedded in a planner, with zero-shot outdoor transfers; FATHOM couples a multimodal recurrent state-space world model with diffusion-based trajectory selection for AUV tracking of sparse light markers, with offline studies and real-AUV experiments indicating accurate belief prediction and robust, real-time tracking under occlusions and visual degradation without motion capture; a reinforcement-learned camera controller for PIV uses only reconstructed velocity fields and uncertainty to position a manipulator-mounted camera, transferring zero-shot from photorealistic simulation to a water tunnel where it frames wakes more accurately and faster than fixed views while using far fewer image pairs; and a learned inertial odometry method for quadrotors augments IMU fusion with body-frame torque dynamics in an EKF, improving pose and velocity estimation over prior learned inertial odometry on unseen trajectories and four held-out public datasets, with ablations indicating rotor-derived torque inputs are most informative.

Whole-body locomotion and manipulation control across diverse robot morphologies are addressed via hybrid model-based/learning frameworks: ForPC trains a locomotion prior and a residual force-aware policy to coordinate humanoid cart pushing using only onboard observations, reducing cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% versus a locomotion-only baseline in sim-to-sim tests and transferring to a Unitree G1 that pushes carts with up to 30 kg payload at 0.5 m/s without real-world tuning; DKWBC decouples humanoid motion tracking and balancing by pairing inverse-dynamics plus PD tracking with a learned residual torque policy, and experiments show a single balancing policy maintains accurate tracking under varying surfaces, payloads, and interactions on both simulation and hardware; SUGARv2 synthesizes interaction references from task templates to train privileged teachers and then distills to visual loco-manipulation policies with shared imitation rewards and domain randomization, reaching a mean 91.0% success across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks in simulation and demonstrating sim-to-real transfer; and a loco-manipulation framework for the COBRA snake robot uses contact-implicit sidewinding trajectory optimization over full dynamics, validated in hardware for pushing objects to goal locations and further tested in simulation for complex robot–object–ground contact handling.

institution_matches.title: Task-Driven Closed-Loop Design Optimization of Passively Morphing Quadrotors for Contact-Mediated Narrow Gap Traversal
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a closed-loop design optimization method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque–deflection response of two passively folding arms by using task success rate in contact-based simulation of narrow-gap traversal as the design objective. institution_matches.title: CS-Pi: Constraint-Satisfying Flow Policy Sampling

institution_matches.title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
institution_matches.overview: Analyzing real human intervention data, the paper finds that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls and often provide suboptimal corrective actions, and proposes a progress-based human intervention model that better matches real-user algorithm rankings than common existing human models. institution_matches.title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning

institution_matches.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
institution_matches.institution: Carnegie Mellon University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Flex-RSI, a benchmark for recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget, where an executor iteratively improves task solutions and an improver revises the agent harness (prompts, tools, memory, and control loop), keeping changes only if validation scores improve. institution_matches.title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics

topic_matches.institution: Anyverse Dynamics; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework in which learned correction codes—combining language guidance, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals—are used both to train and to adapt a vision-language-action policy (A2-WLA) via a correction encoder/adapter and a MetaBrain supervisor, enabling online behavior adjustment without changing core policy weights. topic_matches.title: TPS-A*: Path Planning for Any-Shape Vehicles with Certified Collision Checking in Trajectory Parameter Space
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces TPS-A*, a lattice-based global planner that uses kinematically feasible trajectory generators and a precomputed grid in trajectory parameter space to perform certified collision checking for exact, possibly non-convex vehicle footprints, making per-node collision cost independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count. The authors prove that the parameter-space grid never overestimates the free distance along the continuously swept footprint and that TPS-A* yields collision-free paths with bounded suboptimality relative to its lattice abstraction, exactly reaching goals with or without heading via certified Reeds–Shepp trajectories; an independent exact checker finds no collisions in TPS-A* paths. On 300 cluttered simulated worlds using the true footprint, TPS-A* solves all queries with a collision-free goal pose in a median of 3 ms on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X—comparable in time to hybrid A*, for which 45% of paths overlap obstacles, and nearly 60× faster than a state-lattice planner (the only other collision-free method); with position-only goals it is 89× faster than hybrid A*, and it matches or exceeds hybrid A* in parking and narrow doorway scenarios, docks a non-convex fork footprint infeasible for convex models, and is demonstrated on a real robot navigating a campus among people.

topic_matches.title: SUGARv2: Learning Diverse Visual Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Skills from Synthesized Interaction References
topic_matches.institution: Beihang University; Peking University; ShanghaiTech University
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills that synthesizes interaction references by adapting reusable task templates across spatial configurations, generating coordinated robot–object motion references at low human effort. SUGARv2 trains privileged teacher policies to follow the synthesized references and then learns visual control policies via teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with shared reference-based imitation rewards, augmented by diverse object instances and visual domain randomization for generalization and sim-to-real transfer. Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0% in simulation and successfully transfers whole-body manipulation skills to a real humanoid robot.

topic_matches.title: EGT: Execution-Grounded Traversability through Learned Closed-Loop Trajectory Distributions
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a specific vehicle–controller pair can execute a candidate path while satisfying trajectory-level tracking and progress constraints, and estimates EGT using a latent-space flow-matching model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and a prior over vehicle attitude and wheel–ground contact points. In 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4–39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe-path acceptance to 7.7%, indicating more accurate traversability assessment than traditional margin-based metrics. When integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT lowers navigation failure rates by 24–42 and 30–44 percentage points compared with two prior methods ([1] and [2], respectively) and reduces goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%, with additional zero-shot transfer demonstrations on real-world outdoor terrain.

topic_matches.title: Extended Model-Based Learned Inertial Odometry
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a learned inertial odometry method for quadrotors that uses a body-frame representation and incorporates body-frame torque dynamics, predicting short-horizon relative displacements that are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experiments on unseen quadrotor trajectories show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for pose estimation. Evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets with whole trajectory shapes held out of training reports lower velocity error on every held-out set, and indicates that torque inputs derived from rotor signals are the most informative.

topic_matches.title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
topic_matches.institution: Robbyant; The University of Hong Kong; Zhejiang University
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes DKWBC, a dynamics-informed humanoid whole-body control framework that decouples motion tracking and balancing by combining inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback for tracking with a learned residual policy that provides additional joint-torque corrections for balance. By explicitly modeling motion-dependent torque demands through model-based tracking, DKWBC simplifies the learning task for the residual policy, which only needs to account for balancing corrections rather than full control outputs. Experiments in simulation and on real humanoid hardware show that a single learned balancing policy within DKWBC generalizes across multiple motion datasets and maintains accurate motion tracking and balance under varying ground support conditions, attached payloads, and physical interaction.

topic_matches.title: Autonomous Whole-body Loco-manipulation Using a Snake Robot
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents a whole-body loco-manipulation framework for the COBRA snake robot that enables any body segment to make contact, using a contact-implicit dynamic model that unifies robot-ground, robot-object, and object-ground interactions within a Moreau-Jean time-stepping scheme. A trajectory optimization over the full-order dynamics, guided by a geometric planner and a nominal proportional controller, is formulated to autonomously push an object to a goal location while the robot sidewinds. The planner and controller are validated on hardware across varied configurations, and additional simulations with a simplified trajectory optimization demonstrate the handling of robot-object and object-ground contacts for loco-manipulation.
